en: My father reads the newspaper slowly while he drinks his tea.
tamil: எங்க அப்பா டீ குடிச்சுக்கிட்டே மெதுவா பேப்பர் படிப்பார்.
context: Describing your father's morning habit.
explain: 'Reads' has -s because 'my father' is one person. 'With his tea' shows the time.
usage: Use it when you describe your family to a new friend.
leelaQ: What does your father or mother do in the morning?
answer: My mother makes tea and my father reads the news.

en: Is there any hot water in the bathroom?
tamil: பாத்ரூம்ல வெந்நீர் இருக்கா?
context: Asking at home before a bath.
explain: 'Is there any ...?' asks if something is available. Use it for things you cannot count.
usage: Use it at home on a cold morning or in a lodge.
leelaQ: Do you take a hot bath or a cold bath?
answer: I take a hot bath in winter and cold in summer.

en: I didn't sleep well last night.
tamil: நேத்து ராத்திரி எனக்கு சரியா தூக்கம் வரல.
context: Telling a colleague why you look tired.
explain: 'Didn't' + base verb is the negative past. 'Well' is an adverb here.
usage: Use it at work when someone says you look tired.
leelaQ: How do you feel when you do not sleep well?
answer: I feel tired and cannot focus on my work.

en: The cook comes at ten and leaves by twelve.
tamil: சமையல்காரம்மா பத்து மணிக்கு வந்து பன்னிரண்டுக்குள்ள போய்டுவாங்க.
context: Explaining the house help's timings to a relative.
explain: Two verbs joined with 'and' share the same subject. Present simple shows a fixed routine.
usage: Use it when you tell someone your home schedule.
leelaQ: Does someone help you with the work at home?
answer: Yes, a helper comes every morning to clean.

en: Put your dirty clothes in the basket, not on the floor.
tamil: அழுக்கு துணிகளை தரையில போடாம கூடையில போடு.
context: A mother correcting a child.
explain: 'Not on the floor' corrects the habit. Use a comma before the 'not' part.
usage: Use it at home to teach children to keep the room clean.
leelaQ: Do you keep your room clean and tidy?
answer: Yes, I clean my room every Saturday.

en: Are you coming home for lunch today?
tamil: இன்னைக்கு மதியம் சாப்பாட்டுக்கு வீட்டுக்கு வர்றியா?
context: A wife asking her husband on the phone.
explain: 'Are you coming' asks about a near plan. It sounds natural on a phone call.
usage: Use it on a phone call to plan the day's meals.
leelaQ: Where do you have lunch on workdays?
answer: I have lunch in the office canteen.

en: I usually reach home by half past six.
tamil: நான் பொதுவா ஆறரை மணிக்குள்ள வீட்டுக்கு வந்துடுவேன்.
context: Telling a friend your regular return time.
explain: 'Half past six' means 6:30. 'By' means not later than that time.
usage: Use it when you plan a visit or phone call after work.
leelaQ: What time do you reach home after work?
answer: I reach home around seven in the evening.

en: We had a power cut, so we ate dinner outside.
tamil: கரண்ட் கட் ஆனதால நாங்க வெளியே சாப்பிட்டோம்.
context: Telling a friend about an evening at home.
explain: 'So' joins a reason and its result. 'Had' is the past of 'have'.
usage: Use it to explain a change in your normal routine.
leelaQ: What did you do the last time the power went off?
answer: We sat outside and talked until the power came back.

en: Remember to set the alarm for five thirty.
tamil: அலாரத்தை அஞ்சரை மணிக்கு செட் பண்ண ஞாபகம் வெச்சுக்கோ.
context: Reminding a family member at night.
explain: 'Remember to' + verb reminds someone to do a future task.
usage: Use it at night before an early morning.
leelaQ: Do you set more than one alarm in the morning?
answer: Yes, I set two alarms so I do not oversleep.

en: Mondays are always the busiest day for me.
tamil: திங்கள்கிழமை எனக்கு எப்பவுமே ரொம்ப பிஸியா இருக்கும்.
context: Talking about your weekly routine to a friend.
explain: 'The busiest' is the superlative form. It compares one day with all the others.
usage: Use it when you explain why you have little free time.
leelaQ: Which day of the week is the busiest for you?
answer: Mondays are busy because of the weekly meeting.

en: Why don't you take the metro instead of driving?
tamil: நீ கார் ஓட்டுறதுக்கு பதிலா மெட்ரோவுல போகலாமே?
context: Suggesting a better way to travel to a friend.
explain: 'Why don't you ...?' is a friendly suggestion. 'Instead of' + -ing shows another choice.
usage: Use it with a friend who complains about traffic and parking.
leelaQ: Do you prefer the metro or the bus?
answer: I prefer the metro because it is on time.

en: I will call you after I reach the bus stop.
tamil: நான் பஸ் ஸ்டாப்புக்கு போய் சேர்ந்ததும் உனக்கு கால் பண்றேன்.
context: Telling your wife you will phone on the way.
explain: After 'after', use present simple (reach), not 'will reach'. The main sentence uses 'will'.
usage: Use it on a call when you are leaving home.
leelaQ: What do you do while waiting at the bus stop?
answer: I listen to songs on my phone.

en: He doesn't like waking up early on holidays.
tamil: விடுமுறை நாள்ல சீக்கிரம் எழுந்திருக்க அவனுக்கு பிடிக்காது.
context: Talking about your brother's habit.
explain: 'Doesn't' goes with 'he'. After 'like', use the -ing form.
usage: Use it when you talk about someone who sleeps late on holidays.
leelaQ: What do you do on a holiday morning?
answer: I sleep late, then have a slow breakfast.

en: Could you share your auto with me till the signal?
tamil: சிக்னல் வரைக்கும் உங்க ஆட்டோவுல வரலாமா?
context: Asking a stranger politely for a shared ride.
explain: 'Could you ...?' is polite. 'Till the signal' says how far you go.
usage: Use it when you need a shared ride in a busy city.
leelaQ: Have you ever shared an auto with a stranger?
answer: Yes, I did it once when it was raining heavily.

en: I'm folding the clothes now.
tamil: நான் இப்போ துணிகளை மடிச்சுட்டு இருக்கேன்.
context: Telling someone you are busy at the moment.
explain: 'I'm folding' shows an action happening now. Use it to explain you are busy.
usage: Use it on a call when someone asks what you are doing.
leelaQ: What are you doing right now?
answer: I am answering your question and drinking tea.

en: Have you taken your tablets after food?
tamil: சாப்பாட்டுக்கு அப்புறம் மாத்திரை போட்டியா?
context: Asking an elderly parent about medicine.
explain: 'Have you taken' asks if it is done. 'After food' is common Indian English.
usage: Use it with an elder at home to take care of their health.
leelaQ: Do you take any medicine every day?
answer: I take a vitamin tablet after breakfast.

en: Our lift is not working, so we use the stairs.
tamil: எங்க லிஃப்ட் வேலை செய்யல, அதனால படியில ஏறுறோம்.
context: Explaining an apartment problem to a visitor.
explain: 'Is not working' says it is out of order. 'Stairs' are the steps.
usage: Use it in an apartment when a guest asks about the lift.
leelaQ: Do you live in a house or an apartment?
answer: I live in an apartment on the third floor.

en: I like to relax with a cup of tea in the evening.
tamil: சாயங்காலம் ஒரு கப் டீயோட ரிலாக்ஸ் பண்ண எனக்கு பிடிக்கும்.
context: Telling a friend about your evening habit.
explain: 'Like to' + verb talks about something you enjoy. 'With a cup of tea' is a common phrase.
usage: Use it when someone asks what you do after work.
leelaQ: How do you relax after a long day?
answer: I listen to old Tamil songs with a cup of tea.

en: Where did you keep the iron box?
tamil: அயர்ன் பாக்ஸை எங்க வெச்ச?
context: Looking for something at home.
explain: 'Where did you ...?' asks about a past action and a place. Use 'keep' without -ed after 'did'.
usage: Use it at home when you cannot find something.
leelaQ: Can you find things easily in your house?
answer: Yes, because everything has a fixed place.

en: Tomorrow I'll wake up early and go for a run.
tamil: நாளைக்கு நான் சீக்கிரம் எழுந்து ஓடப் போறேன்.
context: Making a personal promise to a friend.
explain: 'I'll' shows a promise or decision made now. 'Go for a run' is a common phrase.
usage: Use it when you decide to start a healthy habit.
leelaQ: Do you exercise in the morning?
answer: No, but I plan to start next week.

en: Please do not wait for me, start eating.
tamil: எனக்காக காத்திருக்காதீங்க, சாப்பிட ஆரம்பிங்க.
context: Telling the family to eat without you.
explain: A polite negative command and a positive command. 'Start eating' means begin the meal.
usage: Use it on a call when you will reach home late.
leelaQ: Do you wait for everyone before you eat?
answer: Yes, we like to eat together as a family.

en: The tiffin box is in your bag.
tamil: டிபன் பாக்ஸ் உன் பேக்குல இருக்கு.
context: A mother telling her child at the school gate.
explain: 'Is in' tells the place of something. 'Tiffin' is a popular Indian word for light food.
usage: Use it when you remind a child about the food they carry.
leelaQ: What does your child carry for lunch?
answer: My child carries rice and vegetables.

en: It is raining, so I'm taking an umbrella.
tamil: மழை பெய்யுது, அதனால குடை எடுத்துட்டு போறேன்.
context: Getting ready to leave for work in the rain.
explain: Two simple sentences joined with 'so'. 'I'm taking' shows a plan right now.
usage: Use it at the door when you see rain outside.
leelaQ: What do you take with you when it rains?
answer: I take an umbrella and wear a raincoat.

en: Do you want me to drop you at the bus stand?
tamil: உன்னை பஸ் ஸ்டாண்டுல விடணுமா?
context: Offering a lift to a relative.
explain: 'Do you want me to ...?' offers help politely. 'Bus stand' is common Indian English.
usage: Use it with a guest or relative who is leaving.
leelaQ: Do you often help others by giving them a lift?
answer: Yes, I give my neighbour a lift to the station.

en: He had not finished his bath, so we waited.
tamil: அவன் குளிச்சு முடிக்கல, அதனால நாங்க காத்திருந்தோம்.
context: Explaining why you left late with your family.
explain: 'Had not finished' shows one past action was not complete before another one.
usage: Use it to explain a delay caused by someone at home.
leelaQ: Do you wait for family members when you go out?
answer: Yes, we always leave together.
